column1: # boru Language Specification: fn 3-arg single-triple form — `fn input output body`
# Format: input<TAB>expected<TAB>description
# The `fn` word has two signatures (in match order):
#   [(tnot List) Any List]  Function   — the 3-arg single-triple form
#   [List]                  Function   — the spec-list form
# The triple form takes one [input output body] triple WITHOUT the
# wrapping list: `fn x:Integer [Integer] [x mul 2]`. Its input slot is
# constrained to `tnot List`: a list input ALWAYS selects the spec-list
# form (the two forms stay disjoint), so multi-param triples and
# multi-overload fns need the list form. The BODY slot is List-typed —
# a triple-form body is always a `[…]` code list, which keeps the
# greedy 3-slot window from claiming a non-list value as a body in
# mixed/stack arrangements and makes a truncated `fn input output`
# fail loudly. Non-list input/output follow ParseFnDef's abbreviation
# rule (auto-wrap into a one-element list), mirroring afn.
# COMPUTED operands (`fn (2 add 3) [String] ['five']`) are deliberately
# interpreter-only (the compiled unit would bake the check-time carrier
# where the live value belongs); those cases are pinned in
# lang/go/test/fn_triple_compiled_test.go rather than here so the spec
# corpus's compiled-coverage compile failure ratchet (compiled_coverage_test.go,
# ground to its failureCeiling=0 floor) stays untouched.
# §1  basics — named / unnamed params, output abbreviation
def double fn x:Integer [Integer] [x mul 2]  double 5
column3: named single param

column1: def add10 fn Integer [Integer] [10 add]  add10 5
column3: unnamed bare-type param (body reads the stack)

column1: def neg fn x:Integer Integer [x mul -1]  neg 5
column3: bare-type output abbreviation (Integer ≡ [Integer])

column1: def shout fn s:String [String] [s]  shout 'hi'
column3: string param round-trip

column1: def a fn x:Integer [Integer] [x mul 2]  def b fn [[x:Integer] [Integer] [x mul 3]]  a (b 2)
column3: triple-form and spec-list fns coexist

column1: def b quote [x mul 2]  def f fn x:Integer [Integer] b  f 5
column3: a def-bound list fills the List-typed body slot

column1: def f fn x:(Integer tor String) [String] [`v${x}`]  f 5
column3: disjunct annotation on the single param

column1: def f fn x?:Integer [Any] [x]  f 3
column3: optional-suffix param (x?:T) works in the triple form

column1: def f fn x:Atom/q [Atom] [x]  f hello
column3: quoted-atom (/q) param captures the bare word

column1: # §2  form equivalence — triple ≡ wrapped spec list; mirror forms
def w fn [[x:Integer] [Integer] [x mul 2]]  def t fn x:Integer [Integer] [x mul 2]  (w 3) add (t 3)
column3: fn x:T [O] [b] ≡ fn [[x:T] [O] [b]]

column1: def t ([x mul 2] [Integer] x:Integer fn)  t 8
column3: full mirror (stack) form: body output input fn

column1: 7 (fn Integer [Integer] [10 add]) apply
column3: direct paren construction, applied (a paren places the fn — NUR073 clause 3)

column1: # §2b  the SIX spellings of one single-param/single-return signature
# STYLE-GUIDE.md §S1 tells authors to use the spelling with the FEWEST
# square brackets. These rows are why that is a style rule and not a
# semantic one: all six build a `canon`-identical value, so the choice
# among them carries no meaning at all. `boru fmt` collapses only the
# last one (NUR088), which is why the rule needs stating.
def s1 fn x:Integer Integer [mul 2 x]  s1 21
column3: 1 pair — the target form: bare input, bare output

column1: def s fn x:Integer [Integer] [mul 2 x]  s 21
column3: 2 pairs — bracketed output

column1: def s fn [x:Integer Integer [mul 2 x]]  s 21
column3: 2 pairs — whole triple listed, bare in/out

column1: def s fn [[x:Integer] Integer [mul 2 x]]  s 21
column3: 3 pairs — listed triple, bracketed input

column1: def s fn [x:Integer [Integer] [mul 2 x]]  s 21
column3: 3 pairs — listed triple, bracketed output

column1: def s fn [[x:Integer] [Integer] [mul 2 x]]  s 21
column3: 4 pairs — the fully canonical spelling

column1: # That the six are one VALUE, and not merely one answer, is pinned in
# lang/go/test/fn_triple_compiled_test.go — see
# TestFnSignatureSpellingsAreOneValue. It cannot live here: the assertion
# `deq (canon a/v) (canon b/v)` passes a function VALUE to a word, which
# the compiler declines (Stage 3, soundness), and this corpus holds
# failureCeiling = 0. Same split this file's header describes for
# computed operands.
# §3  literal value patterns as the input
def z fn 0 [String] ['zero']  z 0
column3: literal value pattern admits the matching value

column1: def z fn 0 [String] ['zero']  z 1
column3: literal value pattern rejects other values

column1: # §4  negatives — the (tnot List) input rule, the List body rule, type enforcement
def f fn [x:Integer] [Integer] [x mul 2]  f 5
column3: a LIST input selects the spec-list form, which requires triples

column1: def f fn List [Integer] [size]
column3: a bare List type literal input is rejected by (tnot List) — a single List-typed param needs the spec-list form

column1: def f fn List Any [1] end 7
column3: NUR091: the same rejection is LOUD whatever the output slot — `fn` that took nothing raises at the declaration instead of stranding its operands

column1: fn List Any [1]
column3: NUR091: the bare statement raises the same way

column1: def z fn 0 [Integer] 1  z 0
column3: a non-list body does not fill the List-typed body slot

column1: def f fn x:Integer [Integer]  def g 5  g
column3: a truncated triple fails loudly — the List body slot declines the following statement's values

column1: def bad fn x:Integer [String] [x]  bad 5
column3: declared output type is enforced on return

column1: def dbl fn x:Integer [Integer] [x mul 2]  dbl 'a'
column3: declared input type is enforced at the call

column1: # §5  the spec-list form is undisturbed (regression pins)
1 2 3 4 (fn [[x:Integer][Integer][x mul 2]]) apply
column3: a spec list following fn keeps the 1-arg form even with stack values present

column1: 10 20 def f fn [[x:Integer][Integer][x]]  f 30
column3: stack values before `def … fn [list]` are not stolen by the triple sig

column1: def f fn [[x:Integer] [Integer] [x mul 3]]  f 5
column3: plain spec-list form still dispatches

column1: def sub2 fn [[a:Integer b:Integer][Integer][a sub b]]  10 3 (sub2/v) apply
column3: a paren group after the spec list is NOT pre-evaluated early (the triple sig's window closes on the list)

column1: def s quote [[x:Integer][Integer][x mul 2]]  99 s fn 7
column3: mixed form: a stack spec list is NOT claimed as a triple body (99 fails the List body slot); the list form fires with 7 forward

column1: def sw quote [[x:Integer][Integer][x mul 2]]  def f fn sw  4 (f/v) apply
column3: a word-spelled spec list closes the triple window too (pattern prune resolves the binding)

column1: def f fn (quote [[x:Integer][Integer][x mul 2]])  4 (f/v) apply
column3: a paren-spelled spec list closes the triple window (pattern prune tests the collapsed result)

column1: # §6  composition — closures, generics, higher-order use
def make-adder fn x:Integer [Function] [fn y:Integer [Integer] [x add y]]  def add5 (make-adder 5)  add5 3
column3: nested triple-form fns capture lexically

column1: def identity gen [T] fn x:T [T] [x]  identity 42
column3: generic fn via the triple form

column1: # §7  the OUTPUT slot — types, and only types
# The output slot is the sequence of types the returns must MATCH. It is
# never a sequence of values to produce: nothing in it is appended to the
# body. It reads a `name:Type` pair exactly as the input slot does, so the
# two spellings of one declaration cannot mean different things — and a
# literal is a literal TYPE, admitting exactly itself (a value is a type,
# ADR-010). See design/legacy/FN-OUTPUT-SIG.0.ignore for the sugar this replaced.
def si1 fn [s:String i:Integer [convert Integer s]]  si1 '1'
column3: named return, spec-list form

column1: def si1 fn s:String i:Integer [convert Integer s]  si1 '1'
column3: named return, triple form

column1: def w fn [[s:String] [i:Integer] [2]]  def t fn [s:String i:Integer [2]]  (w 'a') add (t 'a')
column3: fn [x:A y:B [b]] ≡ fn [[x:A] [y:B] [b]] in the output slot too

column1: def f fn x:String 22 [22]  f 'a'
column3: a literal output type admits exactly itself

column1: def f fn x:String 22 [33]  f 'a'
column3: a literal output type rejects a different value

column1: def f fn [[Integer] ['ok'] ['ok']]  f 1
column3: a String naming no type is a literal type, not a failed type-name lookup

column1: def f fn [[s:String] [{i: Integer}] [{i:1}]]  f 'a'
column3: an EXPLICIT map still declares a Map-typed return

column1: def f fn [[Integer] ['Integr'] [1]]  f 1
column3: a MISSPELLED type name has the shape of one, so it stays a loud unknown-type error, not a silent literal

column1: def mk fn [[] ['integr'] [1]]  mk
column3: …while a lowercase string could never be a type name, so it IS the literal, and 1 does not match it

column1: # The Implicit flag is what separates the two readings, on BOTH slots: a
# `name:Type` PAIR lowers to a map flagged Implicit and names a slot, an
# explicit `{…}` map does not and IS the type.
def f fn [[{x: Integer}] [Integer] [1]]  f {x:1}
column3: an EXPLICIT map input declares one Map-typed param, not a named binding

column1: def f fn [[x:Integer] [Integer] [x]]  f 9
column3: …while the pair spelling names the param and binds it in the body

column1: # A named return reduces its annotation before resolving, exactly as a
# named PARAM does. Left raw, a parenthesised annotation falls to the
# TAny tail and the declared union enforces nothing.
def f fn [x:Integer y:(Integer tor String) [x]]  f 1
column3: a named union return admits a member of the union

column1: def f fn [x:Integer y:(Integer tor String) [true]]  f 1
column3: …and rejects a value outside it, rather than degrading to a wildcard

column1: def f fn [[Integer] [(Integer tor String)] [true]]  f 1
column3: the unnamed spelling of the same declaration reads alike

column1: # §8  named-type params — every declaration kind agrees (NUR090 retired)
# A type NAME evaluates to its minted node (design/legacy/TYPE-REPRESENTATION.1.ignore
# §N1), so the bare triple form binds the same constraint the wrapped
# spec-list form always did — for every declaration kind in NUR090's table.
def P refine Integer  def x:P 5  def f fn P Any [1]  f x
column3: refine newtype param, bare triple form
